statement: A chronic, adjuvant-free, antigen-specific peptide immunotherapy built from the mapped HLA-restricted immunodominant C9orf72 epitopes (same platform logic as ATX-MS-1467 for myelin peptides in MS) can re-tolerize the autoreactive CD4+ T-cell compartment in C9orf72-ALS: repeated low-dose, costimulation-free engagement of C9orf72-cognate TCRs converts already Th2/Th17-polarized C9orf72-reactive clones toward an IL-10-dominant, Foxp3-independent anergic/Tr1-like state. This raises the protective IL-10 arm of the C9orf72-specific response (already associated with longer survival), lowers the unopposed inflammatory arm, and -- because only C9orf72-cognate TCRs are chronically re-engaged -- leaves Treg number/function and immune responses to other antigens (pathogens, tumours) untouched, unlike broad Treg-expanding regimens (low-dose IL-2, GM-CSF, polyclonal Treg infusion).
mechanism: Loss of peripheral tolerance to C9orf72 lets autoreactive CD4+ clones persist and, absent tolerogenic co-signalling, default to a Th2/Th17-skewed rather than regulatory fate. A chronic, adjuvant-free C9orf72 peptide panel matched to the patient's own HLA-DRB1/DQB1 restriction supplies that missing tolerogenic signal directly to the T cell (bypassing the monocyte antigen-presentation route, whose correction this KB's own prior analysis found insufficient), converting engaged clones to an IL-10-dominant anergic/Tr1 state; the resulting rise in the IL-10-mediated C9orf72-specific response is linked, via the association already in the graph, to slower disease progression, while antigen restriction preserves immune competence elsewhere.

statement: In C9orf72-ALS, C9orf72 loss of function in myeloid cells (monocytes, microglia) drives motor-neuron injury through a cell-intrinsic innate-immune route — impaired STING degradation leading to IL-17A-dependent CD80 upregulation and neuroinflammation — that is mechanistically separate from, and not explained by, the adaptive CD4+ Th2/IL-10 T-cell response the source literature associates with survival. A myeloid/microglia-restricted blockade of IL-17A or CD80 signalling (rather than restoring C9orf72 dosage in myeloid cells, or non-specifically expanding Tregs/boosting IL-2) is predicted to interrupt this innate axis and reduce motor-neuron injury while leaving the protective adaptive IL-10 response, and systemic immune competence against unrelated antigens, intact. The gain-of-function dipeptide-repeat (polyGR) proteotoxicity arm of motor-neuron injury is immune-independent and would not be addressed by this intervention.
mechanism: c1: C9orf72 loss of function in myeloid cells causes impaired STING protein degradation and sustained STING pathway activity (restates verified literature claim C-795). c2 (assumption, inferred bridge, not directly tested in this model): sustained myeloid STING activity promotes IL-17A signalling. c3: IL-17A signalling sustains CD80 upregulation and neuroinflammation/motor impairment in C9orf72-deficient myeloid cells/microglia, with Il17a deletion or anti-IL-17A antibody reversing the phenotype (restates C-789/C-153/C-666, all from the same under-verified source). c4: this CD80-driven neuroinflammation contributes to motor neuron damage, converging on the same endpoint tracked elsewhere in the graph via the separate LOF+GOF proteostasis route (C-507). c5: the proposed intervention — myeloid/microglia-restricted IL-17A or CD80 blockade — interrupts this chain at its effector step. c6: because the target is a broad, antigen-non-specific innate costimulatory/cytokine loop rather than antigen-specific adaptive tolerance, restricting the blockade to the chronically-activated myeloid/microglial compartment is assumed to preserve systemic immune competence better than systemic Treg-expanding or T-cell-costimulation-blocking strategies. c7 and c8 state, respectively, the mouse-to-human translatability gap and the untouched GOF proteotoxicity arm as explicit limitations. This mechanism deliberately does not route through the CD4+ T-cell-mediated damage pathway asserted in C-44/C-773/H-29, because KB claim C-791 (verified quote) shows that pathway's own premise — that the C9orf72-specific CD4+ response is pro-inflammatory — is false; the response is reported as Th2/IL-5/IL-10 (anti-inflammatory).

statement: Pairing antigen-specific C9orf72-epitope peptide priming with a subsequent low-dose IL-2 boost can durably and selectively amplify the IL-10-producing arm of the C9orf72-specific CD4+ T-cell response -- the arm statistically associated with longer ALS survival -- more than peptide priming alone or IL-2 alone, while confining expansion mainly to antigen-experienced clones, thereby limiting the systemic Treg/immune expansion carried by non-antigen-paired regimens already tried in ALS (Treg infusion+IL-2, GM-CSF), and -- if the downstream cytokine-neuroinflammation step holds -- protecting motor neurons from inflammatory injury.
mechanism: C9orf72-epitope peptide priming engages only cognate TCRs on the already Th2/Treg-biased C9orf72-reactive CD4+ clones; a subsequent low-dose IL-2 pulse, acting preferentially through the high-affinity IL-2 receptor transiently upregulated on antigen-engaged cells, is proposed to selectively stabilize and expand the IL-10-producing fraction of that specific population rather than the whole repertoire. This raises the IL-10-mediated C9orf72-specific response, which the cohort data associate with slower progression; mechanistically, Th2/Treg cytokines including IL-10 are reported to dampen microglial neurotoxicity, offering a route from the peripheral T-cell shift to reduced neuroinflammatory injury to motor neurons. No edge in the prior graph is contradicted; this proposal is additive, combining two modalities (antigen-specific peptide, IL-2 boosting) that the graph so far only carries separately and non-combined.
